subject: Bio
title: Nutrition & transport
sub: Photosynthesis and leaves, diet and digestion, transport in plants, the heart and blood
strategyIntro: Cambridge Core Biology is assessed on Paper 1 (40 multiple-choice questions, 45 min), Paper 3 (structured theory questions, 1h 15, 80 marks) and Paper 6 (questions on experiments). Your school test may be shorter, but it will be marked the same way.

strategy.title: Multiple choice
points: About a minute per question. If one is taking longer, mark it and move on.
Cross out options you know are wrong first. Two often look similar: read every word.
Never leave one blank. A wrong answer loses nothing.

strategy.title: Structured questions
points: Marks go to keywords. Write the textbook term: “oviduct”, not “tube”.
The marks in brackets tell you how many separate points to make.
Label diagrams with a ruler line that touches the exact part.

strategy.title: Questions on experiments
points: Results tables: units go in the column headings, not next to each number.
Graphs: label both axes with units, choose an even scale, plot with small crosses.
Know the control variables and one safety precaution for each experiment.

strategy.title: Easy marks people lose
points: Saying plants get food from the soil. They make glucose by photosynthesis; the soil gives water and mineral ions.
Writing “arteries carry oxygenated blood”. Arteries carry blood away from the heart (the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood).
Saying the large intestine digests food. It absorbs water.
Saying transpiration is water “leaving the plant”. Say evaporation from mesophyll cells and diffusion of water vapour out through stomata.

commandWords: Give a short fact. No explanation needed.
Say what happens or what you see. With data, quote figures and units.
Say why or how. Use “because” and link cause to effect.
Apply what you know to a new situation. Any sensible reason scores.
Give similarities or differences for both things in the same sentence.
Show working and give the unit.
quizIntro: Answer in Paper 1 style: about a minute each, eliminating wrong options first. Read the explanation after every answer, even when you get it right.
flashIntro: These are close to Cambridge’s own wording. Say each definition out loud before you tap, then check you used the exact keywords.

flashcards.back: The process by which plants make carbohydrates from raw materials using energy from light.
carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen (in light, with chlorophyll).
Green pigment in chloroplasts that absorbs light energy so it can be used to make glucose.

flashcards.front: Uses of glucose in a plant
flashcards.back: Respiration; stored as starch; cellulose for cell walls; sucrose for transport; with nitrate, amino acids for proteins.
Boil in water, then in ethanol (water bath) to remove chlorophyll, rinse, add iodine: blue-black means starch.
Keeping a plant in the dark for about 48 hours so it uses up its starch before an experiment.
Light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and temperature: the one in shortest supply limits the rate.
Needed to make amino acids (proteins). Lack causes poor growth and yellow older leaves.
Needed to make chlorophyll. Lack causes yellowing between the veins of the leaves.
Column-shaped cells near the upper surface, packed with chloroplasts: the main site of photosynthesis.
Pores, mainly in the lower epidermis, that let carbon dioxide in and oxygen and water vapour out. Guard cells open and close them.
A diet with all the nutrients in the right proportions, plus fibre and water, giving the right amount of energy.
Carbohydrates and fats: energy. Proteins: growth and repair. Vitamins and minerals: health. Fibre: moving food through the gut.
Needed for healthy skin and gums. Lack causes scurvy. Found in citrus fruit.
Needed for strong bones and teeth. Lack causes rickets (soft, weak bones).
Needed to make haemoglobin in red blood cells. Lack causes anaemia (tiredness).
Adds bulk so the gut muscles can push food along (peristalsis); prevents constipation.
Breaking food into smaller pieces without chemical change, e.g. chewing. Increases surface area for enzymes.
Breaking large insoluble molecules into small soluble molecules, using enzymes.
Amylase: starch → simple sugars. Protease: protein → amino acids. Lipase: fats → fatty acids and glycerol.
Movement of small food molecules and ions through the wall of the intestine into the blood. Mostly in the small intestine.
Finger-like folds lining the small intestine that give a large surface area for absorption.
Hydrochloric acid kills harmful microorganisms in food and gives the acid pH the stomach protease needs.
Carries water and mineral ions from the roots to the leaves. Also supports the plant.
Carries sucrose and amino acids from where they are made to where they are used or stored.
Long extensions give a large surface area for taking in water (by osmosis) and mineral ions.
Root hair cells → root cortex cells → xylem → mesophyll cells in the leaf.
Loss of water vapour from leaves: water evaporates from mesophyll cells into air spaces, then diffuses out through stomata.
It pulls water up the xylem, supplying water and mineral ions to the leaves, and cools the leaf.
Higher temperature increases the rate: water evaporates and diffuses faster.
Higher humidity decreases the rate: the concentration gradient of water vapour is smaller.
When a plant loses water faster than it takes it in, its cells become flaccid and it droops.
Put a cut stem (e.g. celery) in coloured dye: the dye shows up in the xylem.
Blood passes through the heart twice in one full circuit: once to the lungs and once to the rest of the body.
Right atrium and right ventricle (pump blood to the lungs); left atrium and left ventricle (pump blood to the body).
Thicker and more muscular than the right, because it pumps blood all round the body at higher pressure.
Stop blood flowing backwards in the heart and veins.
Carry blood away from the heart at high pressure. Thick, muscular, elastic walls; narrow lumen.
Carry blood back to the heart at low pressure. Thin walls, wide lumen, valves.
Tiny vessels with walls one cell thick, where substances are exchanged with tissues.
Contain haemoglobin to carry oxygen. No nucleus, biconcave shape.
Defend against pathogens: phagocytes engulf them (phagocytosis); lymphocytes make antibodies.
Platelets help blood clot. Plasma carries cells, glucose, ions, carbon dioxide, urea and hormones.
Fatty deposits block the coronary arteries. Risks: diet high in saturated fat, smoking, lack of exercise, stress, age, genes, being male.
Heart rate rises so muscles get more oxygen and glucose and carbon dioxide is removed faster.

quiz.q: What are the raw materials for photosynthesis?
quiz.why: Carbon dioxide (from the air) and water (from the soil) are the reactants. Glucose and oxygen are the products.

quiz.q: In the starch test, why is the leaf boiled in ethanol?
options: To remove the chlorophyll so the colour change can be seen
quiz.why: Ethanol dissolves the chlorophyll, so the green colour no longer hides the iodine result. Boiling in water first kills the leaf.

quiz.q: Which leaf tissue contains the most chloroplasts?
quiz.why: Palisade cells are packed with chloroplasts and sit near the upper surface where light is brightest.

quiz.q: A variegated leaf (green and white) is kept in light and then tested with iodine. Only the green parts go blue-black. This shows that photosynthesis needs:
quiz.why: The white parts have no chlorophyll and made no starch, while both parts had the same light and carbon dioxide.

quiz.q: Which mineral ion does a plant need to make chlorophyll?
quiz.why: Magnesium is part of the chlorophyll molecule. Nitrate is needed for amino acids.

quiz.q: A lamp is moved further away from some pondweed. What happens to the number of bubbles per minute?
options: It increases, because it is cooler
It decreases, because light intensity falls
It increases, because there is more carbon dioxide
quiz.why: Further away means lower light intensity, so less photosynthesis and less oxygen given off.

quiz.q: A lack of vitamin C in the diet causes:
quiz.why: Scurvy (bleeding gums) is caused by lack of vitamin C. Rickets: vitamin D or calcium. Anaemia: iron. Constipation: fibre.

quiz.q: Where are most digested food molecules absorbed into the blood?
quiz.why: The small intestine is long and lined with villi, giving a huge surface area for absorption.

quiz.q: Lipase breaks fats down into:
quiz.why: Fats are made of fatty acids and glycerol, so lipase releases those.

quiz.q: How does chewing help digestion?
options: It increases the surface area for enzymes to act on
quiz.why: Chewing is physical digestion: smaller pieces give more surface area, so enzymes work faster.

quiz.q: What is the main job of the large intestine (colon)?
quiz.why: Water is absorbed in the colon. Bile comes from the liver; protein is digested in the stomach and small intestine.

quiz.q: Which order does food pass through the gut?
options: Mouth, stomach, oesophagus, small intestine, large intestine
Mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine
Mouth, oesophagus, stomach, large intestine, small intestine
Mouth, stomach, small intestine, oesophagus, large intestine
quiz.why: Mouth → oesophagus → stomach → small intestine → large intestine → anus. The liver and pancreas add juices but food does not pass through them.

quiz.q: Which tissue carries water up the stem?
quiz.why: Xylem carries water and mineral ions. Phloem carries sucrose and amino acids.

quiz.q: How is a root hair cell adapted for absorbing water?
options: It has a large surface area
It has a thick waxy cuticle
quiz.why: The long hair-like extension gives a large surface area in contact with soil water.

quiz.q: In which conditions would transpiration be fastest?
quiz.why: Heat speeds up evaporation and diffusion; dry air keeps a steep water vapour gradient.

quiz.q: Water vapour leaves a leaf mainly through the:
quiz.why: Stomata are pores, mostly on the lower surface. The waxy cuticle stops most water escaping elsewhere.

quiz.q: What does phloem transport?
quiz.why: Phloem moves sucrose and amino acids around the plant. Starch is insoluble, so it is not transported.

quiz.q: Which blood vessel carries blood from the heart to the lungs?
quiz.why: Arteries carry blood away from the heart: the pulmonary artery takes deoxygenated blood to the lungs.

quiz.q: Why is the wall of the left ventricle thicker than the right?
options: It pumps blood all round the body at higher pressure
It receives blood from the lungs
quiz.why: The right ventricle only pumps to the nearby lungs; the left must push blood round the whole body.

quiz.q: Which part of the blood carries oxygen?
quiz.why: Haemoglobin in red blood cells combines with oxygen in the lungs and releases it in the tissues.

quiz.q: Which vessel has valves and a wide lumen?
quiz.why: Veins carry blood at low pressure, so they need valves to stop backflow and a wide lumen for easy flow.

quiz.q: Which of these increases the risk of coronary heart disease?
quiz.why: Smoking damages arteries and raises blood pressure. The others lower the risk.

quiz.q: What is the function of the valves in the heart?
options: To separate oxygenated and deoxygenated blood
quiz.why: Valves make sure blood flows one way. The septum separates the two sides; the muscle wall pumps.

examIntro: Paper 3 style. Write your answer first, then open the mark scheme and give yourself one mark per point you made clearly. One point per mark is the rule.

exam.q: Write the word equation for photosynthesis.
points: carbon dioxide + water (on the left)
→ glucose + oxygen (on the right)
exam.note: Light and chlorophyll can be written over the arrow.

exam.q: Describe how you would test a leaf to show it contains starch.
points: Boil the leaf in water (to kill it / break membranes)
Put it in hot ethanol in a water bath to remove the chlorophyll
Rinse in water to soften it
Add iodine solution
Blue-black shows starch is present
exam.note: Any 4. Safety: ethanol is flammable, so heat it in a water bath, not over a flame.

exam.q: Describe three ways a leaf is adapted for photosynthesis and explain how each helps.
points: Large surface area
absorbs more light
Thin
short distance for carbon dioxide to diffuse
Many chloroplasts in palisade cells near the top
absorb more light
Stomata
let carbon dioxide in
Air spaces in spongy mesophyll
carbon dioxide diffuses to the cells
Veins with xylem
bring water to the cells
exam.note: Any 3 features with a matching explanation: 1 mark each.

exam.q: Name the deficiency disease caused by a lack of vitamin D and state one of its effects.
points: Rickets
Soft / weak bones or bowed legs

exam.q: Explain why starch must be digested before it can be absorbed.
points: Starch molecules are large / insoluble
They cannot pass through the wall of the intestine into the blood
Amylase breaks starch into small, soluble sugars
Small molecules can be absorbed (in the small intestine)

exam.q: Describe what happens to the protein in a meal as it passes through the stomach and small intestine.
points: Stomach muscles churn the food (physical digestion)
Hydrochloric acid kills microorganisms / gives acid pH
Protease in the stomach starts breaking protein down
Protease in the small intestine breaks it down to amino acids
Amino acids are absorbed into the blood
Through the villi, which have a large surface area
Food is moved along by peristalsis
Loss of water vapour from plant leaves
By evaporation from mesophyll cells and diffusion out through the stomata

exam.q: Describe the pathway taken by water from the soil to a leaf.
points: Enters root hair cells (by osmosis)
Passes through root cortex cells
Moves up the xylem
Into mesophyll cells of the leaf

exam.q: Explain why a plant transpires faster on a hot, dry day than on a cool, humid day.
points: Higher temperature makes water evaporate faster from mesophyll cells
Water vapour molecules have more kinetic energy / diffuse faster
Dry air has low humidity
So there is a steeper concentration gradient of water vapour between leaf and air
More water vapour diffuses out through the stomata

exam.q: State two differences between arteries and veins.
points: Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins carry it to the heart
Arteries have thicker, more muscular / elastic walls
Veins have valves (arteries do not, except at the heart)
Veins have a wider lumen
Arteries carry blood at high pressure; veins at low pressure
exam.note: Any 2. Each must compare both vessels.

exam.q: Explain why heart rate increases during exercise.
points: Muscles contract more, so they respire faster
They need more oxygen and glucose
Delivered faster by the blood
Carbon dioxide must be removed faster

exam.q: Describe the route blood takes from the vena cava to the aorta.
points: Right atrium
Right ventricle
Pulmonary artery to the lungs
Pulmonary vein back to the heart
Left atrium
Left ventricle
Valves stop blood flowing backwards
